title: QTc prolongation
draftNote: Content collected from the user, not yet written up. Kept outside server/data/adverse-effects/ so it is not published. Source [1]: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines 15th ed., Tables 1.35-1.38. Source [2]: Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions, Table 3.1, Boxes 3.4-3.5 and the QT chapter text.

footnotes.lumateperone: Limited clinical experience; an association with QT prolongation may emerge.
footnotes.aripiprazole: One case of torsades de pointes (TdP) and two of QT prolongation reported, and an association with TdP in database studies. Healthy-volunteer data suggest QTc prolongation of about 8 ms. May increase QT dispersion. Low-dose aripiprazole added to another antipsychotic has no effect on QT.
footnotes.olanzapine: Isolated cases of QTc prolongation; acts on the cardiac IKr channel. Other data suggest no effect on QTc.
footnotes.amisulpride: TdP common in overdose; strong association with TdP at clinical doses.

items: Extremes of age: children and elderly may be more susceptible to QT changes

riskFactors.note: Hypokalaemia-related QTc prolongation is more common in acute psychotic admissions. Physical and genetic factors (cardiac potassium channels, CYP enzyme function) may not be found on routine examination but probably predispose to arrhythmia.

groups.extra: Some quinolones affect QTc; see the manufacturer's information.

nonPsychotropics.after: Beta-2 agonists and sympathomimetics may provoke TdP in patients with a prolonged QTc.

rows.action: None, unless T-wave morphology is abnormal
Consider reducing the dose or switching to a drug of lower effect; repeat ECG
Repeat ECG. Stop the suspected causative drug(s) and switch to a drug of lower effect
Review treatment. Consider reducing the dose or switching to a drug of lower effect

definitions.high: Significant average QTc prolongation at therapeutic doses (usually >20 ms)
definitions.moderate: Moderate average QTc prolongation at therapeutic doses (10-20 ms)
definitions.low: Severe QTc prolongation only in overdose, or small average increases (<10 ms)
definitions.none: No known QTc prolongation at therapeutic doses or in overdose

high: Any drug or combination of drugs used in doses exceeding the recommended maximum

psychotropicEffects.cyp450Note: P450 inhibitor, so may prolong QTc when combined with another QTc-prolonging drug.

prescribing.intro: High-quality evidence and consensus on prescribing and monitoring QTc-prolonging drugs are lacking.
considerations: Avoid combining QTc-prolonging drugs; the effect is likely additive.
Use the lowest effective dose and avoid drugs with significant metabolic interactions; QTc prolongation is likely dose-dependent.
Assess cardiac risk (personal and family history, cardiac symptoms, cardiovascular risk factors) before starting any drug with moderate or high QTc effect.
Consider an ECG before starting any QTc-prolonging drug; repeat at steady state or if cardiovascular risk factors are present.
Consider consulting a cardiologist before starting a QTc-prolonging drug if there are cardiovascular risk factors or symptoms suggesting arrhythmia.

ecgScreening.originNote: Box 3.4 summarises NICE guidance. Per site rules, show the criteria without naming the country-specific body.
ecgScreening.before: Offer a screening ECG before starting an antipsychotic known to prolong QTc if:
criteria: Specified in the drug's product information
A cardiovascular risk factor is found on history or examination (e.g. hypertension)
The patient is an inpatient or being admitted
ecgScreening.repeat: Consider repeating the ECG once the therapeutic dose is reached, then yearly.

prescribingScreeningMonitoring: Assess cardiovascular risk and consider a screening ECG
Consult a cardiologist if in doubt
assessment: Bloods plus ECG (with or without 24-hour tape or echocardiogram)
management: Consider stopping or reducing the dose of offending drugs
Refer to a cardiologist if: >500 ms or >60 ms increase; history suggesting arrhythmia; prior cardiac event; unable to stop or reduce the medication

rationalising: Weigh the risk of continuing treatment (QTc prolongation) against the risk of changing it (deterioration in mental state).
Where possible, stop or reduce the dose of the QTc-prolonging drug, particularly when QTc is >500 ms.
Consider changing to a treatment with lower QTc risk.
When in doubt, discuss with cardiology.

nonPharmacological.note: Likely to be done by medical colleagues rather than psychiatrists.
items: Optimise cardiovascular risk (hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, smoking cessation, lifestyle advice).
Optimise other relevant medical conditions (e.g. thyroid disease, heart failure).

monitoring: Repeat ECG 1-2 weeks after any significant dose change.

immediate: QTc >500 ms, or a rise of >60 ms since starting the QTc-prolonging drug
New unexplained cardiac symptoms plus QTc >440 ms (men) or >470 ms (women)

sourceConflicts: Lumateperone (no effect) and pimavanserin (moderate) appear only in [1].
